definition.text: The study of how humans interact with the pedosphere and with key parts of the biosphere, lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere.

facts.text: It is one of the general subfields of edaphology, alongside agricultural soil science, and studies human interaction with the pedosphere beyond crop production.

Its topics include surface water quality, vadose zone functions, septic drain fields, wastewater land treatment, stormwater, erosion control, contamination and remediation, wetland restoration, soil degradation and nutrient management.
It also covers movement of viruses and bacteria in soil, bioremediation, microbes engineered to degrade pollutants, land use, global warming, acid rain and anthropogenic soils such as terra preta.
Much of the research in environmental soil science is done with models.
Soil chemistry's emphasis has shifted toward environmental soil science, whose knowledge is key to predicting the fate of contaminants in soil.

definition.text: The relation between two overlapping terms: soil quality, a soil's fitness for a given purpose, and soil health, a holistic view of soil as a self-sustaining living system.

facts.text: Soil health has largely replaced the older term soil quality, though the two still overlap considerably.
Soil quality meant fitness for a use, such as quality of soil for maize production or for roadbed preparation.
The phrase soil health comes from European organic or biological farming movements, well before soil quality became a discipline around 1990.
Swiss soil biologist Otto Buess's 1978 essay 'The Health of Soil and Plants' largely defines the field even today.

title: Interpretations of soil health

definition.text: The differing ways users define soil health, understood as a soil's condition at a defined place and scale against benchmarks of healthy functioning.

facts.text: Because users weigh a soil's functions differently, the term only makes sense in the context of the user's aims and the boundary of the soil in question.
Ecological landscape assessment and agronomic objectives give potentially conflicting interpretations, each claiming its own criteria; a soil can function well ecologically yet not serve crops.

Benchmarks differ with a soil's inherited qualities and geography; generically, a healthy soil absorbs and cycles well, sheds clean runoff, keeps carbon and productivity near climatic limits and leaks few nutrients.
Unlike soil quality, soil health is not applied to a purpose such as preparing a roadbed.

contested_note: Sources describe many potentially conflicting interpretations, especially ecological landscape assessment versus agronomic objectives.

title: Soil health testing

definition.text: Assessing soil health by measuring the ecosystem services a soil provides against benchmarks, combining physical, chemical and biological analyses.

facts.text: Benchmarks used include CO2 release, humus levels, microbial activity and available calcium.
Testing is spreading in the United States, Australia and South Africa; Cornell University has had a Soil Health Test since 2006, and Woods End Laboratories a soil quality package since 1985.
Both combine aggregate stability, mineral balance and CO2 respiration analyses, now considered hallmarks of soil health testing.
Other labs add biological factors to routine chemical nutrient tests, notably a soil respiration test called the CO2-Burst.
Many labs and scientists resist new biological tests because fertility metrics rest on crop-response models that do not exist for soil health; critics say novel tests may miss management changes.
Over the past 40 years US soils may have lost up to 75% of their carbon (humus), though how much is debatable; critics say old testing models have failed.
Older models stressed maximum yield, while nutrient pollution of US surface and groundwater grew, reported in the early 2000s as the worst since the 1970s.
In practice soil health testing tends to be confined largely to agronomic objectives.

contested_note: Sources report resistance among labs and scientists to new biological tests and call the extent of US soil carbon loss debatable.

definition.text: A concept, introduced by Maharjan and colleagues in 2020, that uses native land in a region as the benchmark for measuring how far managed soils fall short in health.

facts.text: Soil's importance for food security, agro-ecosystems, the environment and human life has shifted research strongly toward soil health.
Without site- or region-specific benchmarks, research on how different agronomic management affects soil health had been limited.

definition.text: The chemical, physical and biological measurements used to judge soil quality, since soil function itself cannot easily be measured directly.

facts.text: Physical indicators measure texture, bulk density, porosity, water content at saturation, aggregate stability and penetration resistance, showing infiltration and water available to plants.
Chemical indicators include pH and nutrient levels; a typical soil test evaluates only chemical properties.
Biological indicators reflect organisms such as earthworms, millipedes, centipedes, ants and spiders, which regulate soil structure, degrade contaminants and cycle nutrients.
Soil quality can be evaluated with the Soil Management Assessment Framework, and in Germany agricultural soil quality is rated on the soil value scale (Bodenwertzahl).
Very few monitoring systems give near real-time indicator data, and almost all of them report only at research level.

title: Soil as a filter and buffer

definition.text: The soil's role in regulating water and in filtering, buffering and transforming materials that move between the atmosphere, plant cover and water table.

facts.text: Soil particles capture contaminants, so water comes out cleaner in aquifers and rivers.
Soil transforms and decomposes waste materials into new materials.
It can store large amounts of carbon as soil organic matter, lowering atmospheric carbon dioxide and helping mitigate climate change.

title: Mapping soil functions

definition.text: Mapping soil properties as interpretations for particular functions, such as food production, environmental protection or civil engineering.

facts.text: Soil mapping identifies, describes and delineates soil types from field observation or from inferences drawn from sources such as aerial photographs.
Maps can show single properties, such as critical nutrient or heavy-metal levels, or combined interpretations such as an erosion risk index.
It extends soil survey, using maps of soil components with pedotransfer functions and soil inference models to infer how mapping units will perform.

distinct_from: Soil as a filter and buffer

definition.text: The ability of a soil to resist destabilising influences or recover its healthy state after them.

facts.text: It is a subset of the broader notion of environmental resilience.
The related term soil resistance is the inherent capacity to withstand disturbance, while resilience is the capacity to recover after disturbance.
It must be seen against pedogenesis, a process taking thousands of years, compared with the short time humans have depended on and changed soil.
Parent material and topography are passive soil-forming factors, while climate and the biosphere are active; variations in the active factors amount to environmental change or shock.
Soils have endured an oxygen-free atmosphere, the arrival of land plants 420 million years ago and, since the last ice age, extended wet, dry and fire periods.
Open questions are whether soil should stay constant or reach a new equilibrium, and how long it can hold out or adjust on pedological time.
Resilience is limited by the rate and extent of human-imposed change compared with the time soil needs to recover.
In Australia, little more than 200 years of European-style farming has brought salinity, acidity, nutrient decline, erosion and structural decline.

definition.text: Creating new soil and restoring soil health by minimizing topsoil loss, retaining more carbon than is lost, boosting biodiversity and keeping water and nutrient cycles working.

facts.text: It is a form of ecological regeneration within restoration ecology, reforming degraded soil through biological, chemical or physical processes.
Its benefits include carbon sequestration against climate change, lower erosion risk and greater overall soil resilience.
Healthy soil is a mix of living organisms, organic matter and inorganic material, with air and water typically making up half its volume.
Plants trade carbohydrates for nutrients released by rhizosphere microbes, a symbiosis that maintains mostly fungal living biomass and raises soil carbon.
For optimal plant growth a carbon to nitrogen ratio of 20–30:1 must be maintained.
Soil biodiversity creates competitive pressure that shrinks the niche open to disease and parasitic organisms.
Organic carbon content is one of the most predictable ways to tell whether a soil has degraded.
Reducing or halting tillage raises topsoil carbon concentrations, allowing the soil to regenerate.

title: Forms of soil degradation

definition.text: The four general ways soil declines in condition under poor management: erosion, and physical, chemical and biological degradation.

facts.text: Erosion displaces soil by water runoff or wind, typically from bare fields; physical degradation changes structure so water and air cannot enter, as in compaction by large vehicles.
Chemical degradation includes contamination with heavy metals or hydrocarbons, acidification, salinization, nutrient leaching and toxins from mining and waste management.
Biological degradation is a loss of biological activity, as when fertilizer buildup inhibits nitrogen-fixing microbes, bringing biodiversity loss, greenhouse gas emissions and less carbon storage.
One third of the globe's land has degraded soil, with around 500 million hectares degraded in the tropics and subtropics.
Excessive tillage, especially ploughing, leaves soil open to wind erosion, and farm vehicles compact it, reducing its permeability to air and water.
Chemical fertilizer suppresses nitrogen-fixing microbes and raises nitrous oxide emissions; replacing lost fertility with more fertilizer creates a positive feedback loop.
Overgrazing removes plant roots, reducing organic content and the symbiosis between plants and the soil microbiome.
Urban construction compacts and seals soils, intensifying storm runoff and erosion, and cities concentrate pollutants that leach into soils.

notes: The one-third share of land with degraded soil (S:66b5eae34558) is another share-of-land estimate; see Global extent of land degradation in degradation-and-desertification.

title: Agricultural soil carbon loss
article: Soil regeneration#Climate change and the carbon cycle

definition.text: The release of soil carbon to the atmosphere through farming and fossil fuel use, which regenerative practices aim to reverse.

facts.text: Some 61 billion tonnes of carbon leave soils each year through decomposition and oxidation of organic carbon, and a similar amount returns through decomposition and plant–microbe symbiosis.
The top two meters of soil hold an estimated 3,012 billion tonnes of carbon, more than the atmosphere (879 billion) and vegetation (600 billion) together.
Since farming began, an estimated 133 billion tonnes of carbon has been lost from soil, mostly in the last two centuries of mechanised agriculture.
Cutting soil emissions reduces overall greenhouse gas emissions, and regenerative practices can act as natural carbon dioxide removal.

title: Regenerative soil practices

definition.text: Farming and management methods, many from conservation agriculture, that regenerate soil and improve its quality.

facts.text: Monoculture depletes soil carbon and nutrients, because each crop takes up or returns only its own set of nutrients.
Cover cropping, crop rotation, reduced soil disturbance, mulch retention and integrated nutrient management increase carbon sequestration and cut fossil fuel use.
Permaculture mimics natural ecosystems with mixed, native and perennial crops and avoids tilling, allowing more sustained contact between soil microbes and roots.
Holistic management, from Allan Savory's work, claims planned grazing can improve soil health and reverse desertification; researchers dispute the desertification claim.
Soil amendments, chosen to suit current soil conditions, sequester toxins, balance pH, add nutrients and promote organisms.

Inorganic amendments improve texture and structure, balance pH and limit heavy-metal availability: alkaline ones include wood ash, ground limestone and red mud, mineral ones gypsum and dredged materials.
Organic amendments such as mulch, compost, biochar, manure and biosolids improve biological activity, water permeability and structure; biosolids are nutrient-rich, so they should be used sparingly.

contested_note: Researchers dispute the claim that holistic planned grazing reverses desertification.

title: Soil governance

definition.text: The policies, strategies and decision-making processes that nation states and local governments apply to the use of soil.

facts.text: Globally it has been limited to an agricultural perspective because of food insecurity in the most populated regions; in the developing world it favours sustainable agriculture and food security.
It differs from soil management, the practices used to raise and maintain soil fertility, structure and carbon sequestration.

It needs collaboration among governments, local authorities, industries and citizens on coherent policies that regulate soil use, avoid conflicts between users and promote sustainable land management.
Concern over farming's effects such as erosion built awareness of soil governance and made science and technology the link between management and governance.
It usually sits within land governance, with little attention to urban and industrial soils, especially in rapidly urbanizing developing countries.
Global soil governance focuses on degradation's effects on food production and on conflict between space for settlements and for farming.
FAO and UNESCO made a global soil map in 1981; a new global soil map, led by ISRIC with GIS and remote sensing, is being built by a scientific consortium.
The International Union of Soil Sciences proposed 5 December as World Soil Day in 2002, and the UN General Assembly designated it in December 2013.

related: International Soil Reference and Information Centre

definition.text: A partnership set up by the FAO and its members in December 2012 to improve governance of the planet's limited soil resources for food security and ecosystem services.

facts.text: Its goal is food security and restored ecosystem services through conserving, enhancing and restoring soils by productive, sustainable use.

It is an open, voluntary partnership of FAO member countries with universities, research centres, soil science societies, UN agencies, NGOs, companies, farmer associations and donors, working through Regional Soil Partnerships.
Its First Plenary Assembly, at FAO headquarters in June 2013, adopted rules of procedure and established the Intergovernmental Technical Panel on Soils.
The panel's 27 soil experts, representing all regions, advise the partnership on science and advocate sustainable soil management.

conflicts.text: The Intergovernmental Technical Panel on Soils was established in 2003.
conflicts.note: S:5fedbc8cc783 says the panel was nominated and established at the First Plenary Assembly in June 2013.

definition.text: The European Union's approach to soil, which it treats as a non-renewable resource while leaving its governance largely to member states.

facts.text: In 2006 the European Commission proposed a soil protection framework to unify rules scattered across EU legislation.
Member states rejected it under the subsidiarity principle, arguing their own strong domestic soil policies sufficed, so the EU has no cohesive soil governance policy.
Healthy soils are part of the European Green Deal, and the EU Soil Strategy for 2030, launched in 2021, aims at healthy soils for food security and climate mitigation.
The strategy frames a Soil Monitoring Law, first meant to be legally binding on soil health, whose final version set no obligatory targets and covers only monitoring.

title: Soil governance in India

definition.text: India's policies on soil, shaped by the weight of agriculture in its economy and by widespread farmland degradation.

facts.text: In 2010 agriculture employed 58.2% of India's workforce and contributed 15.7% of GDP.
Excessive, miscalculated fertiliser use aimed at higher output has left nearly two-thirds of India's farmland classed as degraded or sick.
Gujarat's Soil Health Cards Programme of 2006, which tests farmers' soil and advises on fertilizer and crops, was later extended nationally under the Ministry of Agriculture.

India's National Programme to Combat Desertification builds capacity in soil and water management, micro-credit for women and marginalised groups, alternative energy and land legislation for industry and mining.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
notes: S:08cb3205d35d says India ratified the UNCCD in 1984, but the Convention was adopted in 1994 (S:859b0116a0fd), so the year is likely wrong and is left out.

title: Urban and industrial soil governance
article: Soil governance#Impacts of industrialization and urbanization

definition.text: Governing soils in cities and industrial areas, where industrialization and urbanization are emerging as major causes of soil degradation, especially in the developing world.

facts.text: Industry alters soil chemistry with heavy metals and effluents, while construction and landfills compact and excavate soil, disturbing water purification and storage.

Poor knowledge of soil management and disregard for the environment drive urban soil degradation, and developing countries often lack resources to enforce policies, leaving soil and water heavily polluted.
Urban soil management uses an interdisciplinary approach to protect soil-dependent biodiversity, reduce industrial pollution and make soil more resilient to construction compaction.
In Central Europe an urban soil management strategy, built on networks of universities and municipal authorities, designs soil strategies for selected cities.

title: Soil bioengineering

definition.text: The use of living plant materials, such as seeds, plants and plant communities, to perform engineering functions like stabilizing slopes and controlling erosion.

facts.text: A discipline of civil engineering, it can sometimes replace classical engineering works but in most cases usefully complements them.
Used for many centuries and promoted with European examples by Schiechtl (1980), it is now practised worldwide on eroding and unstable slopes and embankments.
It works wherever its plants grow well, as in tropical, subtropical and temperate zones, and is limited in arid, frost, alpine and arctic regions and in species-poor areas.
Technically, plantings shield soil from wind, rain, frost and flowing water, slow flow along banks, bind soil, trap snow, sand and sediment, and roughen slopes against avalanches.
Ecologically, they improve the water regime, loosen soil with roots, even out temperatures, enrich nutrients on raw soils and raise yields on neighbouring cropland.
They heal landscapes scarred by landslides, wildfires, mining and construction, and fit structures into the landscape.

Such works are not always cheaper to build, but counting service and maintenance over their lifetime they are normally more economical, since they become living systems that maintain themselves by succession.

notes: The Economic effects section both says the works are not always cheaper to build (S:1e705cf1b0bd) and lists lower construction costs (S:c8f3bc40f80e); the fact follows the first.

title: Septic drain field

definition.text: A subsurface wastewater disposal facility, also called a leach field, that removes contaminants from the liquid leaving a septic tank after anaerobic digestion.

facts.text: A microbial ecosystem breaks down the organic materials in the liquid; the drain field, septic tank and piping together make up a septic system.
It typically has trenches of perforated pipe and porous material, often gravel, covered with soil to keep animals and surface runoff away from the wastewater.
Design is both hydraulic, for the volume of wastewater, and catabolic, for its long-term biochemical oxygen demand.
Just as the septic tank is sized for anaerobic organisms, the field is sized to support aerobic soil microbes that turn the tank's anaerobic effluent into aerobic water.
A biofilm on the trench walls uses atmospheric oxygen to break down organic compounds; incompletely oxidized effluent shows as hydrogen sulfide odors or iron bacteria in nearby wells.
Its microbes can barely break down petroleum products and chlorinated solvents and cannot remove dissolved metals, and bleach or sanitizers can slow or stop their activity.
A field with several disposal areas lets one rest while nematodes eat accumulated biofilm and fats, easing bioclogging, though percolation rarely regains its original clean-water rate.
Adding a biofilter lowers the effluent's oxygen demand, though not its volume, so the field can be smaller and more land is left free.

prerequisites: Soil as a filter and buffer

definition.text: Judging whether a soil can receive septic tank effluent, by a percolation test or by reading the soil's morphology.

facts.text: The soil must be permeable enough for effluent to percolate away yet fine enough to hold back pathogenic bacteria and viruses; percolation tests time clean water dispersing from a trench.
Aerobic conditions must kill pathogens before they reach wells or surface water: sand and gravel pass wastewater too fast, while silt and clay filter pathogens but limit flow.
Where seasonal high water tables limit sizing, a soil scientist reads texture, structure, consistency, pore and root distribution, and the colour signatures of water-table fluctuation.
In service, percolation falls as microbial biofilm, fine particles, congealed fats, rising groundwater and frozen ground clog or limit the trench's soil interface.

title: Soil Health Card Scheme

definition.text: An Indian government scheme, launched on 19 February 2015, that gives farmers soil cards with crop-wise nutrient and fertiliser recommendations based on soil tests.

facts.text: It promotes soil-test-based, balanced fertiliser use so farmers get higher yields at lower cost; experts identify the soil's micronutrient deficiencies and suggest remedies.
The government allocated ₹568 crore (US$61 million), and the 2016 Union budget gave states ₹100 crore (US$11 million) to make cards and set up labs.
By July 2015 only 34 lakh cards had been issued against a 2015–16 target of 84 lakh; by 16 May 2017, 725 lakh cards had been distributed.
Its national form followed Gujarat's Soil Health Cards Programme of 2006, which was credited with helping the state's farm growth reach three times the national rate in 2009.

conflicts.text: The 2015–16 target was 104 lakh soil samples.
conflicts.note: S:ffa6e198594b gives a 2015–16 target of 100 lakh soil samples.

notes: The lead's targets of cards for 14 crore farmers (S:42e718694a49) and results shown on the cards (S:df7d2dde1a18) carry citation-needed tags and are left out.

definition.text: Returning damaged land to some degree of its former state after industry, natural disasters or other harm.

facts.text: Mining, farming and forestry often degrade land; in parts of the United States, reclamation means returning disturbed land to an improved state.
Mine rehabilitation contours waste dumps against erosion, caps sulfide ore with clay to stop acid forming, and covers landfills and tailings with topsoil or soil and vegetation.
Australian mine rehabilitation bonds total $9.49 billion, and reclaiming abandoned US mines is estimated to cost $9.6bn.

title: Septic tank

definition.text: An underground concrete, fibreglass or plastic chamber where household sewage settles and is anaerobically digested as primary treatment.

facts.text: Solids settle and are digested in the first chamber; the liquid then goes to a septic drain field, which needs a percolation test to show the soil is porous enough.
Sludge builds up faster than it decomposes, so it is pumped out by vacuum truck, every few years in some systems and every 10-20 years in others.
Tanks remove little nitrogen; soils usually retain the phosphorus, but sandy soils near water can become saturated with phosphate and pass it on, risking eutrophication.
About 20 percent of US households relied on septic tanks in 2008, but dense development can push groundwater pollution beyond acceptable limits.

prerequisites: Soil as a filter and buffer

definition.text: Modifying mined land to restore it to an ecologically functional or economically usable state.

facts.text: In open-cut mines, rock backfills the pit, stored pre-mining soil goes on top, then topsoil, and finally vegetation is restored.
The original landscape cannot always be restored; usually the limit is the physical and chemical stabilization of mine waste.
The Forestry Reclamation Approach calls for a loosely graded, uncompacted rooting medium at least four feet deep of topsoil or weathered sandstone.
Under the US Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, operators file a reclamation plan and a bond before mining; a coal tax funds abandoned-mine reclamation.

title: Permaculture

definition.text: An approach to land management and settlement design that copies arrangements seen in flourishing natural ecosystems.

facts.text: Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined the term in 1978; its three ethics and Holmgren's twelve design principles are widely cited.
Common practices include Hügelkultur (burying wood to hold soil water), sheet mulching, no-till gardening, keyline design and vermicomposting.
It has been largely isolated from science and criticised as pseudo-scientific or poorly defined.
Some 21st-century studies support claims that it improves soil quality and biodiversity; a 2024 review said it strongly enhances carbon stocks and soil quality.

contested_note: Critics call it pseudo-scientific and ill-defined, while recent studies report gains in soil quality and carbon.

title: Ecosystem service

definition.text: The many benefits that people derive from ecosystems, such as clean water, food, decomposition of wastes and flood control.

facts.text: The UN Millennium Ecosystem Assessment popularized four categories: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services.
Supporting services, such as nutrient cycling, primary production and soil formation, make possible others such as food supply, flood regulation and water purification.
Regulating services include waste decomposition and detoxification, and erosion regulation affects people indirectly through environmental conditions.

New York City restored its Catskill watershed, where soil absorption and filtration, roots and soil microbes brought water back to standard, for $1–1.5 billion instead of a $6–8 billion filtration plant.
Evaluations of ecosystem services may assign them an economic value.

related: Soil as a filter and buffer

title: Active carbon

definition.text: A newer soil health measurement of active carbon, the most readily usable portion of a soil's total organic carbon.

facts.text: Active carbon contributes greatly to the functioning of the soil food web.
It joins established soil health measures such as microbial biomass and activity, enzymes, soil organic matter, total nitrogen, available nutrients, porosity, aggregate stability and compaction.

Active carbon is the fraction of soil organic matter oxidized by potassium permanganate, measured with an inexpensive spectrophotometer; it responds quickly to management so it is an early indicator of soil health gains.

notes: The phrase dossier also listed 'permanganate oxidizable carbon' (POXC), but no crawled sentence names the permanganate method; the entry is limited to what the urban agriculture page says.; Extends existing entry.

definition.text: A wastewater system that treats and disposes of effluent on the property that produces it, where there is no public sewer.

facts.text: Most are conventional: a septic tank plus a subsurface infiltration system; such systems handle about 25% of domestic wastewater in the US.
Decomposition by natural organisms remains the main disposal mechanism, so minimum retention times and distances to surface water and wells are set.
Site evaluation characterizes soils, slopes and local hydrology and geology to set the design and placement of system components.
Septic systems are the third most common source of groundwater pollution in the US, failing through poor siting, design or maintenance.

title: Holistic management

definition.text: A systems-thinking approach to managing resources, first developed by Allan Savory for grazing management and now applied to other complex social, ecological and economic systems.

facts.text: Its decision framework tells managers to define the whole being managed, set goals, watch the earliest signs of ecosystem health such as bare ground, use any of eight tools (including grazing, animal impact, fire and rest), and test every decision.

Savory's principles hold that nature works as a community, that removing keystone species such as large herds has wide effects, that livestock can substitute for lost herds, and that timing is the key factor in land use.

Evidence is disputed: a 1972-2016 meta-analysis and a 2022 review of 22 farm-scale studies found no productivity gain, while defenders say trials miss its goal setting and monitoring, and some studies show soil gains.

A 2016 Swedish study put the real carbon sequestration rate of improved grazing management at seven times lower than Savory's claims, and one 2011 study found multi-paddock grazing stored slightly less soil carbon than excluding livestock.

contested_note: Peer-reviewed studies dispute whether holistic planned grazing outperforms continuous grazing or sequesters carbon at the rates its founder claimed.

definition.text: Inherent soil quality is a soil's natural ability to function, while dynamic soil quality is how the soil changes with the way it is managed.

facts.text: Inherent properties change little: a sandy soil drains faster than a clayey one, and a deep soil gives roots more room than a soil with bedrock near the surface.
Management can change dynamic properties such as organic matter, soil structure, and water and nutrient holding capacity.
Soils respond differently to the same management because of their inherent properties, so how those properties vary across the landscape should be considered.

definition.text: Plant roots take up phosphorus dissolved in the soil solution, mostly as phosphate ions, at very low concentrations.

facts.text: Phosphorus in soil solution is far lower than other macronutrients such as sulfur and calcium, from 0.001 mg/L in infertile soil to 1 mg/L in heavily fertilized soil.
The phosphate ion form depends on pH: H2PO4 dominates in strongly acid soils (pH 4 to 5.5), while alkaline soils hold mostly HPO4.

Phosphorus leaves soil through plant removal, erosion of particles that carry it, dissolved surface runoff and leaching, and optimal crop yields may need fertilizer input to exceed removal in the harvest.

definition.text: Potassium is abundant in most mineral soils, yet little of it is easily exchangeable, and it is lost by leaching and by heavy plant uptake.

facts.text: Leaching of potassium can be reduced by raising the soil's cation exchange capacity, and liming an acid soil to raise pH also cuts leaching losses.
Plants take up large amounts of potassium, so biomass removal is a major loss, made worse by luxury consumption, in which plants absorb more soluble potassium than they need.
Readily available potassium, exchangeable on colloids or dissolved, is only 1-2% of the total, while potassium in primary minerals is unavailable and nonexchangeable potassium is slowly available.

definition.text: A quick field test that estimates soil nitrate-nitrogen by shaking a soil sample with water and reading a color test strip.

facts.text: The test shakes a soil subsample 1:1 by volume with distilled water, filters it, puts drops on a strip and reads the color change after 60 seconds, estimating nitrate-N in ppm.
Nitrite rarely occurs in measurable amounts in soil, so the nitrite pad reading is not recorded.
The strip reads at most 50 ppm; a sample at the limit is diluted with equal drops of water and the reading multiplied by 2, or by 4 if diluted again.
Pounds of nitrate-N per acre follow from ppm, sampling depth, and bulk density, which can be assumed to be 1.1 g/cm3 for garden topsoil and 1.5 g/cm3 for subsoil.

definition.text: A fertilizer's grade gives the percentage by weight of nitrogen, phosphorus as P2O5 and potassium as K2O it contains.

facts.text: A 15-10-10 fertilizer holds 15% N, 10% P2O5 and 10% K2O by weight, so the nutrient in a bag is its weight times the percentage.
Elemental amounts convert from oxide forms by factors: P = P2O5 x 0.44, P2O5 = P x 2.29, K = K2O x 0.83 and K2O = K x 1.21.
To work out how much fertilizer to apply, one needs the nutrient rate per unit area, the grade and the area, and for manure the N available in the season, with a rule of thumb of 60%.
Worked example: to supply 2 lb N per 1,000 sq ft with a 30-0-0 fertilizer, divide the rate by 0.30 to get fertilizer per 1,000 sq ft, then multiply by 150 for 150,000 sq ft.

definition.text: Farmers say soil health and scientists say soil quality, and both mean how well a soil functions for the use being considered.

facts.text: Soil health stresses the human influence of years of intensive management, as distinct from inherent differences from parent material and climate, much as a person's health depends on how the body is treated.
Farmers recognize good soil by its dark, crumbly look, higher yields for less effort, less runoff and erosion, and the lower power needed to run machinery than on compacted soil.
A healthy soil has enough nutrients all season, good tilth, stable structure that aids infiltration and water storage, and enough depth before a compact layer or bedrock.
It drains well enough for timely field work, lets oxygen in and carbon dioxide out of the root zone, and has exceptions such as flooded soils for cranberries and paddy rice.

It has low disease, parasite and weed pressure, many beneficial organisms such as earthworms, bacteria and fungi, and no harmful chemicals, whether natural, like soluble aluminum or excess salts, or human-made, like fuel oil or toxic sludge.
A high-quality soil also resists degradation and is resilient, recovering quickly after unfavorable changes such as compaction.

definition.text: Building soils means turning a degraded or low-quality soil into a high-quality one through understanding and sustained action that mirrors natural soil building by plants and organic matter.

facts.text: Some problems are easy to fix, such as liming an acid soil, but a shallow soil can hardly be deepened and a clay subsoil that causes poor drainage needs tile drainage at significant economic and environmental cost.

Soil organic matter benefits almost all healthy-soil characteristics, even pest management, so its management is the foundation of high-quality soil, along with limiting compaction and managing nutrients.
General approaches are to minimize tillage and disturbance, add diverse organic materials, and keep live roots through rotations and cover crops with varied root systems.
Further steps are to keep the soil covered with cover crops or residue against rain and temperature extremes, manage traffic to protect structure, and manage pH and nutrients without polluting water.
In arid regions the sodium or salt in the soil should also be reduced.

definition.text: Scorecards and laboratory tests rate soil health on scales, using field observations of the soil and of the crops growing on it.

facts.text: In the field one can check earthworms, erosion, ease of tillage, structure and color, compaction, water infiltration and drainage, and then rate the crop's appearance, growth rate, root health, drought resistance and yield.
Farmers are advised to fill out a scorecard for each major field or soil type every few years, or send soil to a laboratory offering soil health analyses.

title: Soil nutrient and organic matter cycle

definition.text: Plants and soil organisms cycle organic matter and nutrients, which lets soil keep supporting life.

facts.text: Soil is mineral particles, water, air and organic matter; the nutrients in the particles are locked in crystals, and soil water with carbon dioxide slowly dissolves them by chemical weathering into the soil solution.

Plants capture carbon by photosynthesis and absorb water and nutrients, storing them in biomass; when plants die or are eaten, organisms decompose the residues and manure, making nutrients available again.

Soil stores organic matter because clays bond with organic molecules and aggregates shield particles from decomposers, building a nutrient and energy reservoir, best in deep-rooted prairie and steppe soils.

Plowing broke this cycle by speeding decomposition so more organic matter was lost than returned and nutrients left with the crop; fertilizers later replaced the nutrients but replacing the lost carbon was mostly ignored.
Organic matter forms aggregates that give water storage and gas exchange: mineral particles and pores form the soil's structure, but organic matter mostly makes it fertile.

definition.text: Cultivated soils become worn out when tillage breaks aggregates, organic matter is lost faster, and erosion, compaction and nutrient decline follow.

facts.text: Soils with lower organic matter and weaker aggregation erode faster, and erosion removes organic-rich topsoil, starting a downward spiral of compaction, poor infiltration and root growth, and nutrient decline.
Irrigation in arid regions can make soils saline, so salts in the water must be leached beneath the root zone.
Tropical rainforest soils can degrade within two or three years of conversion to cropland, which is why slash-and-burn developed, while Great Plains soils took many decades to show degradation.
Degradation has cut yields on about 20% of the world's cropland and 19-27% of grasslands and rangelands, and most agricultural soils are in fair, poor or very poor condition.
Some 30-40 billion tons of topsoil are eroded from the world's croplands each year.
The productivity loss led either to colonial ventures to feed the citizenry, like the Romans invading the Egyptian breadbasket, or to the decline of the civilization.
Fertility lasted for centuries only in convergence zones such as valleys and deltas where nutrients and sediments flow together.
Rapid soil degradation in the temperate forests of the eastern United States pushed agriculture westward.

definition.text: The soil-plant-human health connection is the chain by which soil condition affects plant health and plant health in turn affects people.

facts.text: Soil affects people directly too: dust storms from bare soils can cause respiratory problems and lung damage, and frequent early contact with soil and farm animals is linked to fewer allergies and a stronger immune system.

Crops remove nutrients that natural systems recycle; synthetic fertilizers mostly replace nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and calcium but not trace minerals, especially where farmers apply standard blends without soil analysis.

Some soils are naturally low in elements such as selenium, which affects animals and humans more than plants; others become toxic through pollution, cadmium-rich fertilizers or Bangladesh tube-well irrigation that put arsenic into rice.
The largest effect of soil degradation is lost capacity to produce enough nutritious food, especially for rural families in developing countries who eat from their own farms.

Mineral deficiency is rare in developed societies because diets come from many regions, and proving soil-health effects on human health is hard because of dietary complexity and ethical limits on trials.

title: Organic food and human health

facts.text: Plants take up nutrients almost entirely as inorganic forms, so there is no evidence that nutrients from organic sources affect human health differently than synthetic ones.
Some studies find higher antioxidant levels in organic food, but because organic eaters usually have better diets, lifestyles and incomes, no study has tied this to better health outcomes.

contested_note: Whether better soil management and organic production improve human health outcomes is debated, and studies cannot separate confounding factors.

definition.text: Soil physical, chemical and biological properties are linked, so a problem in one often causes problems in others and soil must be managed as a whole.

facts.text: Compaction removes large pores, so large organisms such as earthworms cannot move or survive, and waterlogging can denitrify nitrate to N2 and the greenhouse gas N2O.
Sodium-rich soils common in arid climates have aggregates that break apart, leaving few pores for air exchange and drainage.
Low organic matter and poor structure limit plant growth even when nutrient supply is optimal.

definition.text: Undisturbed natural systems are stable and rebound quickly from fire, wind or excess rain, and their traits give a model for farming.

facts.text: They use energy efficiently through food webs, capture and use rainfall, and cycle nutrients, which keeps the ecosystem from running down and protects water quality.
Rain enters porous soil instead of running off, recharging groundwater and releasing water slowly to streams.

High aboveground and soil biodiversity supplies nutrients and checks disease, as competition and antagonisms such as antibiotics keep soilborne pathogens from causing disease in natural grassland or forest.
Efficiency and diversity make natural systems nearly self-sufficient, needing only sunlight and rain, while crop production disturbs them to favour one or a few species.

definition.text: An approach that grows healthy plants with strong defenses, suppresses pests and enhances beneficial organisms by improving habitat both aboveground and in the soil.

facts.text: It is proactive and preventive, creating conditions that minimize reactive responses; routine soil fumigation or broad-spectrum herbicides create dependency on purchased inputs, weaken resilience and promote resistance.
Aboveground practices include resistant varieties, suitable planting density, variety blends, perimeter trap crops and flowering strips for beneficial insects.

Soil practices: minimize disturbance and compaction, keep soil covered with residue, perennial forages and cover crops, maximize biodiversity, manage water, and keep pH and nutrients in range by routine testing.
A vigorous winter legume cover crop, such as crimson clover in the southern US or hairy vetch in the north, can supply all the nitrogen for the next crop.
Complex rotations with different plant families and sod crops left undisturbed for years are central; tillage buries residue and breaks aggregates, leaving soil prone to erosion.

title: Soil practices that suppress pests

facts.text: Rotation reduces disease, insect, nematode and weed pressure; avoiding excess inorganic nitrogen limits insect damage, and adequate calcium or potassium lowers some crop diseases.
Less compaction lowers insect and root-disease damage, and composts low in available nitrogen but with active organic matter reduce root rot and leaf disease severity.
Cover crops, especially in reduced tillage, keep mycorrhizal spore counts high, and selected cover crops suppress parasitic fungi and nematodes; cereal rye residue reduces weed seed germination.
Reduced tillage and surface residue keep weed seeds on the surface where ground beetles, rodents, ants and crickets eat them, and biologically active soils reduce weed seed numbers.

related: Natural suppression of plant pests in soil

facts.text: A perimeter trap crop intercepts a pest; for example, Blue Hubbard squash around summer squash intercepts striped cucumber beetles.
In East African push-pull, Desmodium legume within corn rows repels stem borers (push) and perimeter grasses attract adult moths (pull), while also supplying nitrogen and suppressing weeds.

title: Plant defense signaling to beneficial organisms

definition.text: Plants under attack release chemical signals that recruit natural enemies of their attackers.

facts.text: Damaged plants produce extra-floral nectar that feeds beneficials and airborne volatiles that guide small wasps to a caterpillar host, in which the wasp lays eggs that kill it.

Roots of some corn varieties attacked by western corn rootworm release a chemical that attracts a nematode killing the larvae; breeding lost this trait in US corn but wild relatives and European varieties retain it.
Neighbouring plants can sense chemicals from wounded leaves and start making defenses before being attacked.

title: Induced resistance in plants

definition.text: Plants form hormones and defence proteins in response to signals from microorganisms, making the whole plant resistant to pathogens even far from the infection site.

facts.text: Systemic acquired resistance follows exposure to a pathogen or even a non-pathogenic organism and involves salicylic acid and defense proteins protecting against many pathogens.
Induced systemic resistance follows root exposure to plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria and involves the hormones jasmonate and ethylene.
Some organic amendments induce resistance, but no reliable, cost-effective indicator yet shows whether a soil or amendment is strengthening plant defense.
Defenses in depth include rhizosphere bacteria that compete with or antagonize pathogens, endophytes inside roots that produce antifungal chemicals, and the plant's own chemicals.

related: Plant defense signaling to beneficial organisms

facts.text: Healthy, thriving plants defend themselves better, while drought, nutrient limits or compaction stress them and make them signal weakness to pests.
Developing optimal soil health is the basis of crop pest management and should underpin integrated pest management programs.

definition.text: Symphylans are white, centipede-like soil arthropods that feed on root hairs and rootlets and damage many crops.

facts.text: Unlike most soil pests they thrive in soils rich in organic matter, since good structure and old root channels let them move easily; they occur in spotty, circular patches in some fields.
Biological activity is not thought to be an adequate defense; potatoes and beans are damaged less, transplanted tomatoes do better than direct seeded, and denser squash planting helps maintain yield.
Organic amendments should be imported with care so the pest is not introduced by accident.
Farmers are often told to incorporate residues because they can harbour pathogens, yet the book promotes surface residue and reduced tillage.

The difference is the system: with rotations, conservation tillage, cover crops and organic additions, soil biological diversity and beneficial organisms increase and crop stress falls, reducing disease pressure, whereas in traditional systems a pathogen more easily dominates.

definition.text: A soil health assessment identifies specific soil problems, tracks change after management shifts and helps value land.

facts.text: It can target problems such as phosphorus deficiency or surface compaction, and show over several years whether cover crops, a new rotation or reduced tillage are improving the soil.
Well-managed healthy soil should be worth more when sold or rented, since it produces more with fewer purchased inputs, which gives an incentive to invest in management.
Assessment works at three levels of detail: general field observations, field assessments using qualitative indicators, and quantitative soil health tests.

definition.text: Observations made in the field, such as cover, crusting, ponding, aggregates, hardness, color, roots and organisms, show a soil's health and its key limitations.

facts.text: The NRCS Cropland In-Field Soil Health Assessment Worksheet rates soil cover, residue breakdown, surface crusts, ponding, penetration resistance, water-stable aggregates, structure, color, roots, biological diversity and biopores.
Measurements vary with moisture and season: a hard soil after a dry spring may be soft after a wet one, and earthworms go deeper in dry spells, so sample at least 10 spots and avoid headlands.
Soil health is best measured in early spring and late fall when moist; problems such as runoff or drought stress show better in wet or dry periods.
Crusting, ponding, slaked patches downslope and rills or gullies signal poor aggregate stability, runoff and erosion, but their absence proves little because they appear only after hard rain.
Soil color reflects mineralogy, oxidation and organic matter; within one soil type darker generally means better, but adding organic matter may take years to change color.
Gently drop aggregates from the top 3 to 4 inches into jars of water and see whether they hold or slake; a soil that seals readily has unstable aggregates.
If broken-up aggregates also stay dispersed in suspension, high sodium may be a problem, usually in arid and semiarid regions.
A spade test checks structure: a good plow layer is fluffy with granules of about a quarter inch, and subsoil clumps should come apart easily into aggregates of several inches.

definition.text: Laboratory soil health tests add biological and physical indicators to chemical ones to assess the soil processes that support ecosystem services.

facts.text: Standard chemical tests alone gave a chemical bias that favoured quick-fix fertilizer use; as of 2020 no single standard soil health test exists, though all agree it needs biological, physical and chemical indicators and interpretation by climate and texture.
Aggregate stability reflects infiltration, crusting and tilth and responds fast to reduced tillage, cover crops or manure; available water capacity depends more on texture than on management.

Soil organic matter is often the single most important indicator but changes too slowly; active carbon, oxidized by potassium permanganate, responds quickly, and soil protein also responds, especially with more legumes.

Soil respiration integrates microbial abundance and activity and tracks nitrogen mineralization potential; the bean root rot bioassay gauges root health and disease pressure from nematodes and fungi such as Fusarium, Pythium and Rhizoctonia.
Salts and sodium should be tested in arid regions and greenhouses, and heavy metals, radioactive materials, solvents and petroleum products in urban or industrial soils.

A report such as the CASH test gives each indicator a measured value and a score of 1 to 100, lists constraints where scores fall below 20, and gives an overall 1 to 100 score useful for tracking change.

A typical northeastern grain field scored well chemically but poorly on physical and biological indicators, since the farmer kept nutrients and pH optimal while intensive cropping unbalanced the soil.
Chemical test values relate to likely crop response, whereas biological tests compare harmful with beneficial organisms, such as plant-feeding versus organic-matter-feeding nematodes.

definition.text: In soil with high biological diversity and activity, inoculating seeds or transplants with beneficial organisms usually brings little advantage, except that legume seed should still get its rhizobia.

facts.text: Interest is growing in microbes that make growth hormones, help plants resist disease and pests, reach water and nutrients or cope with drought and wet stress, but no general recommendations exist.
Inoculants may help in stressful settings: low organic matter, dry or moderately to highly saline soil, and newly farmed fields, especially urban soils.
Dipping transplants in mycorrhizae may pay off if no cover crop was grown that year, particularly after a brassica, which forms no mycorrhizal association.

definition.text: Soil health practices work best combined, since each affects the others, and should be matched to the needs and opportunities of the farm.

facts.text: Practices that improve soil health generally also improve farm economics through higher, steadier yields and lower inputs, but the return may take a few years and may need equipment such as new tillage tools and planters.

Big changes suit strategic moments, such as a new planter or good prices; before planting an orchard, vineyard or landscape, or switching to no-till, add organic matter, relieve subsoil compaction and correct nutrient deficiencies.
Soil health management is a long-term commitment with no silver bullets, needing integration of physical, biological and chemical processes.

title: Soil health balance sheet

definition.text: Soil health management can be pictured as a bank account in which practices that build soil health are credits and practices that degrade it are debits.

facts.text: Credits include manure additions, reduced tillage and cover crops; debits include compaction from field traffic and intensive tillage.
Farming systems differ in their balance sheet: daily harvesting forces traffic on wet soil and small-seeded crops need intensive tillage in the row.
An unavoidable bad practice should be balanced with a good one, or its impact reduced, for example by confining traffic to certain lanes.

distinct_from: Reduced tillage and residue for soil organic matter

title: Reduced tillage and residue for soil organic matter

definition.text: Reduced-tillage systems with residue left on the surface make it easier to maintain soil organic matter.

facts.text: Less disturbance keeps biological activity and organic matter decomposition near the surface and keeps a structure that lets rain infiltrate quickly.
Surface residue or mulch encourages earthworms, keeps soil moist and moderates temperature extremes.
Minimum tillage greatly reduces erosion compared with conventional tillage, and contour tillage, contour strip cropping and terracing also help keep organic matter.
Rotation matters even more under heavy surface residue, which can harbor insects and disease organisms; problems can be worse in no-till monoculture.

definition.text: Holistic soil health management aims to prevent problems, as preventive medicine does, and diagnoses problems by observation and testing.

facts.text: What suits an operation depends on soils, climate, enterprise, region, markets and goals, so tests guide the targeting of constraints but give rarely a simple recipe.
The book advises regular testing of each field every two to three years, preferably with comprehensive soil health analyses, and amendments only when needed.
Keeping test records lets changes be followed over the years and practices fine-tuned.

title: Short- and long-term fixes for soil constraints

definition.text: Management guidelines for soil health constraints are grouped into short-term or intermittent responses and long-term approaches.

facts.text: Short-term recommendations give quick responses and may need repeating, while long-term approaches give no quick fix but address the concern more sustainably.
The same practices are often recommended for different constraints because they address several concerns at once.
Recommendations for physical and biological constraints are less precise than for nutrients because those systems are more complex and the research base is weaker.

For low aggregate stability the short-term fix is fresh organic materials and the long-term fix is reduced tillage, surface mulch and sod rotation; for low available water capacity it is stable organic materials such as compost, lignin-rich residues and biochar.

title: Soil health management on grain farms

definition.text: Grain farms export many nutrients and usually lose organic matter, yet their wide choice of equipment makes it easy to adopt reduced-tillage systems.

facts.text: Well-drained coarse soils suit no-till, and finer-textured soils do well with strip-till or zone-till; travel should happen only when soil is dry enough to resist compaction.
No-till on easily compacted soils is hard because few options relieve compaction; controlled-traffic farming is promising but may need new equipment and GPS guidance.
Even with minimum tillage, rotations with perennial grass or legume forages, or small grains in a corn-soybean system, improve soil health and open space for cover crops.

distinct_from: Short- and long-term fixes for soil constraints

title: Soil health management on vegetable farms

definition.text: Vegetable farms find soil health management especially hard because crops are compaction-sensitive, pests are demanding and land has long been worked hard.

facts.text: Most vegetable farms lack livestock, so fresh organic matter must be brought in as manure, compost, leaves, grass clippings or food waste compost, checked for contaminants.
The shorter main cropping season leaves time for pre-, mid- or post-season cover crops, and mulch from them keeps fresh-market produce off the ground, reducing rot.
Cover or rotation crop choice is critical: bean root rot is suppressed by rapeseed, crown vetch, wheat and rye but enhanced by white clover.

distinct_from: Short- and long-term fixes for soil constraints

title: Soil health management on fruit farms and landscapes

definition.text: Perennial fruit crops and landscapes stay in place for decades, so soil problems must be addressed before planting.

facts.text: For tree and vine crops, evaluation should look at deeper layers for hardpans, subsoil acidity and shallow water tables, since fruit quality is strongly influenced by deep roots.
One-time investments such as drainage, in-row deep ripping and deep lime and compost incorporation are difficult after planting.
After establishment, the emphasis is on the surface layer: avoiding compaction and keeping good surface mulches.

title: Terroir

definition.text: Terroir is the complex interaction of soil, climate and vine that shapes wine.

facts.text: The best wines tend to come from soils that are not overly fertile and that permit some water stress; high organic matter and nitrogen cause excess vegetative growth and reduce fruit set.
Mild water stress and reduced root growth between bloom and ripening increase anthocyanin pigments, which add to wine taste and colour.
Many top wine soils are deep, calcareous, sandy or gravelly and low in organic matter, while poor drainage and aeration harm quality.

title: Six Cs of soil health management

definition.text: The 6C practices are compaction reduction, conservation tillage, continuous living plants, cover crops, crop and animal diversity, and composts and amendments, six practices that build soil health and protect against degradation.

facts.text: Practices that maintain soil health protect the soil against threats, diversify or perennialize annual cropping, and build soil carbon.
The six practices all start with C to stress the role of carbon in soil health.
They can be used singly or combined, and in combination they interact in varying ways; at a long-term Ontario site, soil health scores rose as more of them were adopted.
The main degradation threats they address are erosion, compaction, organic matter decline, nutrient depletion or excess, biodiversity loss, salinization, desertification and contamination.

title: Continuous living plants

definition.text: Keeping living plants growing as continuously as possible, mainly by perennializing cropping systems, protects soil, diversifies systems and builds soil carbon.

facts.text: Natural forests and prairies keep a continuous plant cover and litter layer, whereas annual systems leave periods with no living plants and prairie fallow was shown early on to lower soil organic matter.
Plants allocate roughly 40% of net photosynthetic carbon to roots, and perennials give more carbon input than annuals because of larger root systems and a longer photosynthesis period.
Roots and their microbial communities improve aggregation and hydraulic conductivity; in dry regions they raise porosity and water retained at field capacity.
Longer plant growth and transpiration from deep in the profile also help reduce salinity, because cover and roots limit evaporation and upward salt movement.
Annual systems can approximate it with winter annuals such as winter wheat or fall rye, fall and spring cover crops, relay cropping or intercropping, perennial forages and agroforestry.

distinct_from: Six Cs of soil health management

title: Biodrilling

definition.text: Biodrilling, or biological tillage, uses plant roots to create channels through compacted soil layers.

facts.text: If left undisturbed by tillage, the bio-pores left after roots die and decompose let later crops reach soil below the compaction layer.
Three factors make it work: roots must grow when soil is moist, species differ in root pressure, and macropores must be left intact by avoiding tillage.
Tap-rooted forage radish had about twice as many roots as fibrous-rooted cereal rye at 15 to 50 cm depth under compaction.

distinct_from: Six Cs of soil health management

title: Why soil compaction is hard to reduce

definition.text: Compaction persists because field work is often forced onto wet soil and farm equipment keeps getting heavier.

facts.text: Larger farms must cover more ground, so seeding, spraying or harvesting may happen when conditions are too wet.
Monitoring axle loads and tire inflation and avoiding wet-soil field work help avoid compaction.
Subsoiling with a chisel plow is costly in fuel and time, must be done when soil is dry enough to fracture the plow pan, and needs repeating after a few years if the causes are unchanged.

distinct_from: Six Cs of soil health management

title: Visual soil health assessment

definition.text: Visual soil assessment judges soil health indicators in the field by eye and simple tools, giving quick results mainly on surface soil and physical attributes.

facts.text: It generally takes under an hour with a spade and water; examining a sample coarsely shows texture, aggregation, structure, compaction and infiltration.
With simple tools it can also address pH, respiration and earthworm counts, and score cards with visual keys guide non-experts.
Visual assessments alone cannot judge how well ecosystem services perform, so they work best with analytical tests; CAT scans can measure porosity, connectivity and crusting.

distinct_from: Six Cs of soil health management

title: Soil health scoring curves

definition.text: Soil health scoring turns each indicator into a relative score using a curve, then averages the scores, with higher meaning healthier.

facts.text: Indicators should be interpreted against reference values taken from an undisturbed soil, a highly productive soil, or the distribution of samples from comparable land uses or regions.
Scoring curves have three shapes: more is better (soil organic matter), optimum is best (nutrients, pH) and less is better (salinity).
Curve shapes come from expert opinion or literature; with regional datasets such as Cornell CASH, scores of 0 to 100 show rank within that region.
A criticism is that a soil can score high yet not support plant growth, so it would not by definition be healthy.

title: Soil functions and ecosystem services

definition.text: Soil functions describe what the soil does, bundles of attributes and processes, and its capacity to function powers the ecosystem services it provides.

facts.text: Soil health or quality is commonly defined as the capacity of a soil to sustain biological productivity, environmental quality, and plant, animal and human health.
No single measurement quantifies soil health; it must be inferred from many attributes, processes and contexts.
Example indicators: aggregate stability and organic matter for erosion control; infiltration rate and available water capacity for water supply; respiration and organic carbon for climate regulation.

title: Organic amendments and soil health

definition.text: An organic amendment is any carbon-based material added to soil, and compost is one that has been partially decomposed before application.

facts.text: Added carbon improves infiltration, water holding capacity, microbial activity, cation exchange capacity and nutrient availability; carbon applied over time relates positively to soil organic carbon.
Composting is aerobic microbial decomposition needing managed oxygen, moisture, temperature and C:N ratio; it cuts volume by about 50% and, at high temperature, reduces pathogens.
Composted manure releases more nutrients in years 2 and 3 than in the year applied, so timing relative to crop uptake matters.
Degraded soils gain most, so amendments can be targeted to sandy knolls or compacted areas; effects can last decades and offset erosion damage.
Main constraints by source: pathogens in manure and biosolids, salts in food waste, N and P immobilization from wood waste.

title: Food and Agriculture Organization

definition.text: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) is a specialized agency that leads international efforts to defeat hunger and improve nutrition and food security.

facts.text: It was founded on 16 October 1945 in Quebec City and is headquartered in Rome; it has 194 members, 193 countries and the European Union.
It helps coordinate improvements in agriculture, forestry, fisheries and land and water resources, giving technical assistance and collecting agricultural data.
With the World Health Organization it created the Codex Alimentarius Commission in 1961 to develop food standards.

notes: Institution kept as a summary entry for its soil programmes (Global Soil Partnership, FAO soil classification already have entries).
